blocks.text: bristled with its hair. And Matron, in the Parodies quoted by Athenaeus in book 14, describes hens served at a banquet,
Ἄτριχας, οἰετέας, λαγάνοις κατὰ νῶτον ἐΐσας, [Atrichas, oieteas, laganois kata nōton eïsas,]

Hairless, equal in age, like flat cakes on the back. Hairless, that is, featherless. Nor is there any need to restore ὄτριχας [otrichas] with Casaubon, because that is the reading in the verse of Homer to which he alludes, Iliad 2, line 765. For the parody [παρῳδία, parōdia] consists precisely in this, that a similar word, not the same one, is substituted. Many examples make this plain. So, just as the feathers of hens are called hairs, so too are those of eagles. Hence Tertullian, near the end of his book On Penitence, speaking of King Nebuchadnezzar: his hair, through neglect, displaying an eagle-like shagginess. For this Pamelius substituted leoninum [lion-like], as if an eagle could not be said to bristle with hair. This is refuted by what we have already shown, that the feathers of birds too are reckoned under the name of hairs. And indeed, since Micah (ch. 1, v. 16) says that eagles grow bald, why could not the Prophet Daniel have attributed hairs to them? Certainly the same catachresis [κατάχρησις, katachrēsis] occurs in both places. For baldness is properly the falling out of the hair of the head. [col. 167] Meanwhile the corruption of the passage of Daniel is not recent, since besides the Arabic translator it is followed by Theodoret on Daniel, by the author of the Questions attributed to Justin, Question 44, and by those who wrote the Lives of the Prophets under the names of Epiphanius and Dorotheus, who, though spurious and pseudonymous [ψευδώνυμοι, pseudōnymoi] writers, are nevertheless fairly ancient. Now, if you compare these three passages, first that of the Psalmist, you will renew your youth like the eagle; second that of Isaiah, For those who hope in the Lord their strength will be restored, their wings will grow again like eagles'; third that of Daniel, His hairs grew like those of eagles ^{(4)}: you will see that all of them concern the feathers of eagles, which are restored after moulting [ψίλωσιν, psilōsin]. Hence the eagle comes to seem more vigorous, and so even younger. Nor would it be absurd to join to these the passage of Job about the hawk, chapter 39, verse 26: Is it by your understanding that יאבר נץ, the hawk grows its feathers, spreading its wings toward the south? That is, so that during that moulting [ψιλώσει, psilōsei] it may be revived by the gentle warmth of the sun, and new feathers may more easily grow back in place of those it has lost.
